Understanding the approach

Flexibility is the aim, not constant comfort.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, usually pronounced as the word act, focuses on psychological flexibility. That means being able to contact what is happening and choose actions connected with values, even when difficult thoughts or feelings are present. It is not a promise that distress will vanish or an argument that symptoms do not matter.

The model brings together acceptance, cognitive defusion, present-moment awareness, self-as-context, values, and committed action. These are connected processes rather than six steps everyone completes in a fixed order. A clinician may use discussion, metaphors, or experiential exercises to make them understandable.

Acceptance concerns making room for internal experience when fighting it is not helping. It does not mean approving mistreatment, abandoning medical care, or staying in danger. A person can acknowledge fear and still take protective action; flexibility includes responding realistically to the situation.

Sources act psychotherapy

In plain language

Values are directions, not a performance standard.

Caring, learning, and connection describe ways of acting. A goal can be completed; a value can guide many choices, including small ones and changes of plan.

A worked example

Waiting to feel confident can keep an important conversation on hold.

A fictional example about a safe, ordinary workplace request.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

What matters

Rae wants to discuss a workload that has become unsustainable. They value doing careful work and having enough energy for life outside it.

02

The condition

Rae decides they can speak only when they feel certain the manager will respond well. Because certainty never arrives, the request keeps being postponed.

03

A flexible possibility

An ACT-informed conversation could explore how to make a thoughtful request while allowing uncertainty to be present, rather than making certainty the entrance requirement.

What would acceptance change, and what would it leave unchanged?

Rae might notice the thought that asking will go badly without treating it as a forecast. Values can help clarify why the conversation matters, and practical planning can address how to make it responsibly. The aim is not to enjoy anxiety or pretend the manager has no power.

The workplace still needs to be assessed realistically. If raising a concern carries a genuine risk, seeking advice, support, or another route may be the more values-consistent action. Acceptance of a feeling is not consent to an unsafe situation.

Sources act psychotherapy

Go a little deeper

The ACT processes in everyday language.

These descriptions explain the framework. They are not a self-treatment sequence or a test of whether you are flexible enough.

01Acceptance and defusionMake room for an experience and loosen its control over action.Read more +

Acceptance involves a willing relationship with internal experience where that is useful. Defusion involves noticing thoughts as thoughts rather than automatically obeying or arguing with them. Neither process requires believing a thought is unimportant.

A realistic concern may need action. The question is whether your relationship with the thought leaves room to evaluate and choose.

02Present-moment awareness and perspectiveNotice what is here without reducing yourself to one experience.Read more +

Present-moment work can help distinguish the actual situation from mental replay or prediction. Self-as-context is ACT language for a perspective from which changing thoughts, feelings, and roles can be noticed.

These ideas should be explained in terms that make sense to you. They are not claims about a separate inner entity or a required spiritual belief.

03Values and committed actionConnect the direction you care about with behavior you can review.Read more +

Values clarification asks what qualities you want to bring to life, not what a therapist thinks you should want. Committed action translates those directions into steps that can be adjusted as circumstances change.

Persistence is not the same as rigidity. Rest, boundaries, or changing a goal may also express a value.

Sources act psychotherapy

Inside the work

From a struggle with experience to a more workable response.

01

Understand what is getting in the way

Explore the concern, its effects, and what you have tried. The clinician considers assessment and safety alongside the ACT perspective.

02

Notice the response pattern

Consider what happens when you try to avoid, control, or argue with an internal experience, and whether that response helps over time.

03

Clarify a valued direction

Identify what matters in your own terms and how it could guide a realistic choice.

04

Try, review, and adapt

An experiment is considered in context. The outcome informs the next step rather than proving that you did the approach correctly or incorrectly.

Sources act psychotherapy

Fit, choice and limitations

Acceptance is not resignation. Action is not a demand to push through.

A values discussion must remain yours

Values should not be used to pressure someone into a relationship, a work demand, or a therapist's preferred lifestyle. Disagreement about the meaning of a value is something to discuss, not evidence of resistance.

Symptoms and circumstances still matter

ACT does not make clinical assessment, medical care, accessibility, or material support unnecessary. A practice should be adapted or stopped when it is destabilizing or does not serve the agreed plan.

Sources act psychotherapy

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

How does ACT differ from CBT?

ACT belongs within the broader behavioral therapy landscape. It often emphasizes changing the relationship with thoughts rather than evaluating every thought's accuracy. CBT can include other ways of working with beliefs and behavior. A clinician should explain the actual plan rather than present the labels as a simple either-or.

Does accepting anxiety mean I stop trying to feel better?

No. Relief can matter, but ACT asks whether pursuing control over every feeling is restricting important parts of life. The work can consider both distress and meaningful participation, without promising either on a fixed schedule.

What if I do not know my values?

That uncertainty can be explored through ordinary examples: moments that felt meaningful, choices you respect, or ways you wish to relate to others. Values are not a quiz with a correct list of answers.

Are metaphors and mindfulness mandatory?

No single exercise should be treated as a requirement for every person. Ask how the clinician adapts language, accessibility, and practice. An unfamiliar metaphor is useful only when it clarifies something.

What counts as progress?

A meaningful difference might involve more choice, a less restrictive response to distress, or actions that fit your priorities. Progress should be reviewed against your goals and functioning rather than the ability to use ACT terminology.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
